mcqs.question: A `StockPrice` class calls `chart.update()`, `portfolio.update()`, and `alert.check()` directly by name whenever the price changes. What breaks first as the app grows?
options: Nothing breaks — direct calls are always the fastest option and should be kept
The update methods must all share an identical return type
Adding a fourth dependent requires editing StockPrice again, and it now imports UI components it has no business knowing about
StockPrice can no longer be unit tested under any circumstances
mcqs.explanation: Hardcoding calls means the subject must be edited for every new dependent and ends up importing types it conceptually shouldn't know about. Direct calls can be fast, but the real cost here is coupling and rigidity, not test impossibility or a return-type constraint that doesn't exist.

mcqs.question: A subject has five observers, each of which needs a different subset of the subject's internal state after a change. Which observer model fits best, and why?
options: Push, because sending all data to all observers is always simpler to implement
Pull — a signal-only notification plus a callback into the subject lets each observer fetch only what it needs
Neither model works when observers need different data; a shared broadcast struct is required
Push, because pull models cannot scale beyond one observer
mcqs.explanation: Pull fits when observer needs vary: the subject just signals 'something changed,' and each observer calls back to fetch exactly the subset it cares about, avoiding both under- and over-serving a fixed push payload. Pull scales to any number of observers, and a universal broadcast struct isn't the only option.

mcqs.question: A `PriceChart` component is destroyed when a user navigates away but never called `unsubscribe()`. What's the consequence?
options: None — destroyed components are automatically removed from the subject's observer list
The subject's setPrice() will now throw an exception on every call
The observer list silently deduplicates itself and self-heals
The subject still holds a live reference to the destroyed component, so it can't be garbage collected and still receives updates
mcqs.explanation: The subject's observer list is a live reference; without an explicit unsubscribe tied to the component's teardown, the reference lingers, the object can't be garbage collected, and it keeps receiving update() calls it can no longer meaningfully act on. There's no automatic cleanup or self-healing.

mcqs.question: Inside its `onPriceChanged()` callback, `PriceAlert` calls `stockPrice.setPrice()` again to apply a correction while the original notification loop is still running. What's the risk?
options: Observers later in the original iteration may see a different price than earlier ones, or the list may change mid-iteration if an observer (un)subscribes inside update()
There is no risk — observer callbacks always run in complete isolation from the subject
The subject automatically batches nested setPrice() calls into one notification
JavaScript/TypeScript will throw a compile-time error for this pattern
mcqs.explanation: Mutating the subject from inside a notification callback can trigger a nested notify() while the outer one is still iterating, so different observers can end up reacting to different states, or the observer list itself can shift mid-loop. No such automatic batching or compile-time protection exists — this must be handled by treating callbacks as read-only or queuing follow-up changes.
